title: 中国、標準語起源は人口30万人のまち　発音訓練で首都経済に貢献
extracted_text:
4月を迎えて学校や職場で中国語の学習を始める人も多いだろう。日本人の大半が学ぶ中国語は「普通話」と呼ぶ標準語だが、実は北京の人が話す言葉とは少し異なる。現在の標準中国語の起源をたどるべく、発祥の地である地方都市を訪ねた。

「普通話のふるさと」。北京市より北東に約150キロメートル離れたところにある河北省承徳市の灤平県に入ると、赤い文字が刻まれた石碑が現れる。人口約30万人のこの地方都市は標準中国語の発祥の地として知られる。

「こっちで遊ぼうよ」「いらっしゃいませ、ご注文は」。同地域を巡って驚いたのが、街中で普通に暮らす子どもから高齢者までさながら中国国営中央テレビ（CCTV）のアナウンサーのような聞き取りやすい言葉を話すことだ。地元出身の女性は「私たちの言葉は他と違ってなまりがない。声調（声の高低変化）の発音も正確だ」と誇らしげだ。

なぜこの地の言葉が標準語の起源となったのか。明の時代の初期、モンゴル人の侵略を受けて灤平県の住民は全員、北京やその周辺に移住した。住人のいない状態が200年ほど続き、残っていた地元の方言はこの間にほぼ消滅した。

やがて清朝になると当時の官僚の共通語だった「北京官話」を話す人々が無人の灤平県に移り住んだ。北京官話は発音の正確さや明瞭さから、現在の標準語に最も近い言葉とされる。その後も他の方言の影響をほとんど受けず、土着の言葉として残った。

建国後の1950年代に政府関係者は標準語を定めるため各地に出向いて言葉の音声収集を始めた。灤平県でも3つの村で録音作業を実施した。そのうちの一つ、金溝屯村では7人の村民が対象に選ばれた。

参加者の一人で小学生だった石俊勇さんはのちに中国国営新華社のインタビューで「先生に事務所に呼ばれ、見知らぬ人たちの前で教科書を読んだ。読み終えると皆が褒めてくれた」と振り返っている。当時は何のための作業かわからなかったが、のちに教師として働き始めた時に本当の目的を知ったという。

村のある小学校の敷地内には標準語の音声収集地であることを記念した石碑が残っているという。村には今も中央政府の役人や研究者などが言語の歴史や成り立ちを学びに足を運ぶ。

灤平県は標準語の普及に一役買っている。政府機関や都市部のサービス業など標準語が必要になる仕事に従事する人のための養成所を開いていて、全国から多くの人が集まる。職業訓練などを通じて標準語を身につけた人を21年以降、地元だけでなく北京や天津などに少なくとも3500人以上を送り込んだ。

中国語は日本語と違って、標準語と発音が大きく異なる方言が全国各地に多数ある。地元愛が強く方言を大切にする風習も相まって独特のなまりがあり、中国人同士でも聞き取れないケースも多い。

たとえば標準語に近い北京語にもいくつか特徴があり、単語の語尾などに巻き舌の音を付けて発音するのが代表例だ。記者は日本の大学で標準語を学んだが、中国に住み始めてからは過去に習った覚えのない巻き舌の多用やなまりには日々困惑している。

ほかにも抑揚の幅の狭さが特徴の上海語や、香港やマカオ、広州などで使う広東語が有名だ。いずれも標準語とは発音が全く異なり、別の言語にさえ聞こえる。政府系シンクタンクの中国社会科学院によると、これらを含む主要方言は10あり、それ以外に各地で話されている方言も含めるとその数は100を超えるという。

中国ではほかにもモンゴル語やウイグル語など中国語と系統の違う言語も使われている。

中国語は海外でも多く利用される言葉だ。標準中国語の利用者は約11億人と、英語に次いで世界で2番目に多い言語となっている。英語圏では「マンダリン」、東南アジアなどでは「華語」とも呼ばれる。

中国政府は標準語である普通話の普及を目指している。国内には56の民族が存在し、各地で固有の言語や方言が存在する。言葉の隔たりを解消して意思疎通を円滑にするため、教育では小学校から基本的に普通話を使って授業をする。政府統計によると25年の全国での普及率は85%となる見通しで、00年と比べて30ポイント超上昇する。

灤平県は現在、少子高齢化や結婚、仕事を理由とした他地域からの人口の流入増により、現地に残る純粋な「普通話」を話せる人が減りつつあるとされている。標準語の普及と同時に、各地の言葉の継承も課題となっている。
translated_text:
With April arriving, many people are starting to learn Chinese at schools and workplaces. The Chinese that most Japanese people study is called "Putonghua," or Standard Chinese, but it actually differs somewhat from the language spoken by Beijing residents. To trace the origins of current Standard Chinese, we visited the local city where it all began.

"The hometown of Putonghua." Upon entering Luanping County in Chengde City, Hebei Province, located about 150 kilometers northeast of Beijing, a monument inscribed with red characters comes into view. This local city with a population of approximately 300,000 is known as the birthplace of Standard Chinese.

"Let's play over here" "Welcome, may I take your order?" What surprised us as we traveled around the area was that people of all ages, from children to elderly residents going about their daily lives in the city, spoke in such clear, understandable Chinese—like announcers on China Central Television (CCTV). A local woman proudly said, "Our language is different from others—there's no accent. Our tone (pitch variations) pronunciation is also accurate."

Why did the language of this area become the origin of Standard Chinese? In the early Ming Dynasty, following Mongolian invasions, all residents of Luanping County relocated to Beijing and surrounding areas. The area remained uninhabited for about 200 years, during which time the local dialect that had survived nearly vanished.

Then, during the Qing Dynasty, people who spoke "Beijing Mandarin," which was the common language among officials at the time, moved to the uninhabited Luanping County. Beijing Mandarin is considered the language closest to today's Standard Chinese due to its accurate and clear pronunciation. Thereafter, it remained largely unaffected by other dialects and persisted as the local language.

In the 1950s after the founding of the People's Republic, government officials traveled around the country to collect speech samples to establish Standard Chinese. Recording work was conducted in three villages in Luanping County. In one of them, Jingoutun Village, seven villagers were selected as participants.

Shi Junyong, who was an elementary school student at the time, later recalled in an interview with Xinhua News Agency: "I was called to the teacher's office and read textbooks in front of strangers. When I finished reading, everyone praised me." At the time, he didn't understand what the exercise was for, but later, when he started working as a teacher, he learned the real purpose.

Within the grounds of an elementary school in the village, there is reportedly a monument commemorating the site where Standard Chinese speech was collected. To this day, government officials and researchers from Beijing visit the village to study the language's history and origins.

Luanping County has played a role in spreading Standard Chinese. It operates training institutes for people who need Standard Chinese for their work—in government agencies, urban service industries, and other jobs. Many people come from all over the country. Through vocational training, more than 3,500 people have been placed in jobs in Beijing, Tianjin, and elsewhere since 2021, not only locally but also in these major cities.

Unlike Japanese, Chinese has numerous dialects across the country that differ greatly in pronunciation from Standard Chinese. Coupled with the strong local pride and tradition of preserving dialects, there are unique accents that even Chinese people themselves sometimes cannot understand.

For example, Beijing dialect, which is close to Standard Chinese, has several characteristics—representatively, adding a rhotic sound to word endings and other positions. The reporter studied Standard Japanese at a Japanese university, but since starting to live in China, they have been daily perplexed by the frequent use of rhotic sounds and accents they never learned in their past studies.

Other notable dialects include Shanghai dialect, characterized by its narrow intonation range, and Cantonese, used in Hong Kong, Macau, and Guangzhou. All of these have pronunciations completely different from Standard Chinese and can even sound like entirely different languages. According to the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, a government-affiliated think tank, there are ten major dialects, and including the various regional dialects spoken across the country, the total number exceeds 100.

In China, other languages unrelated to Chinese, such as Mongolian and Uyghur, are also spoken.

Chinese is also widely used overseas. With approximately 1.1 billion users, Standard Chinese is the world's second most spoken language after English. In English-speaking countries, it is called "Mandarin," while in Southeast Asia it is referred to as "Hua Yu."

The Chinese government aims to promote the spread of Standard Chinese, Putonghua. There are 56 ethnic groups in the country, each with their own languages and dialects. To bridge linguistic gaps and facilitate smooth communication, education primarily uses Putonghua from elementary school onward. According to government statistics, the national penetration rate is expected to reach 85% in 2025, an increase of over 30 percentage points since 2000.

Currently, Luanping County is seeing a decrease in the number of people who can speak pure "Putonghua" due to low birth rates, aging, and population inflow from other regions for marriage and work. Along with the spread of Standard Chinese, preserving the various local languages has become an issue.
title_en: China: Hometown of Standard Chinese is a City of 300,000 People - Contributing to Capital's Economy Through Pronunciation Training
